newsitem.title: USA: Dollar surges to highest vs yen in four years.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges to highest vs yen in four years.

text.p: The dollar surged to its highest level in over four years against the Japanese yen Monday, with the strong currency supporting stocks and bonds.
At 11 a.m. EDT, the dollar was trading at 125.72 yen, up from 124.27 late Friday, and its highest level against the Japanese currency since January of 1993.
The dollar also firmed to its highest level since mid-March against the German mark, rising to 1.7111 against Friday's closing rate of 1.6860.

"We did close the dollar very well on Friday and the fact that the dollar went up further against the yen despite a wider-than-expected Japanese current account surplus is noteworthy," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Expectations of higher interest rates in the United States, persistently low Japanese rates and fresh questions about Germany's commitment to a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for monetary union entry combined to help the dollar to its highs, dealers said.

The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was up 17/32 of a point, or $5.3125 per $1,000 face value, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, fell to 7.08 percent from 7.12 percent Friday.

The strong currency and bond markets supported stocks. The Dow Jones industrial average was up 50 points at 6,576, adding to the market's gain late Friday, which reversed sharp losses earlier in the week.

Helping the dollar and Treasuries were heavy capital outflows from Japan, dealers said. The market had expected Japanese corporations to reverse some of the yen repatriation that occured in advance of Japan's fiscal year-end on March 31.
With Japan's new year under way, there was evidence of such a reversal in the form of heavy japanese buying of Treasury bonds, dealers said.
Also lending the dollar support against the yen was the subdued tone of U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's trade rhetoric on Friday.

In Japan on his way to this past weekend's meetings of Asia-Pacific finance ministers, Rubin rejected suggestions that a stronger Japanese currency -- and thus a weaker U.S. dollar -- was the best way to avoid a renewed rise in Japan's trade surplus.
Traders said these remarks helped the dollar shrug off reports of a 15.4 percent rise in Japan's current account surplus for February on Monday.
